newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Patten urges China to adopt, not disrupt HK system.
newsitem.headline: Patten urges China to adopt, not disrupt HK system.

text.p: Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten urged future ruler China on Thursday to adopt rather than meddle with the territory's successful system of free enterprise and democratic government.
Beijing takes control of the city from Britain in an historic handover on June 30.
"This is not some gimcrack community that can be content with gimcrack institutions," the governor told an audience of more than 600 Hong Kong business leaders.

Patten was preaching to the converted in an address to an AmCham (American Chamber of Commerce) luncheon in the city, but his remarks were clearly aimed at mainland Chinese leaders with whom he has been debating the territory's post-handover future.
China has pledged to keep Hong Kong's free, capitalist system for 50 years but doubts have arisen over its commitment to preserving civil liberties and democracy.

"Indispensable to maintaining a well-tuned, high performance economy (in Hong Kong) will be a light hand, keeping out the political pressures and special interests, being guided by the good discipline of the market," the governor said.

"What happens when politicians get a hold of an economy, what happens when an economy becomes a kind of joint venture between politicians and the private sector? Look around the region where the conditions exist: you get endemic corruption."

Hong Kong's status as the world's eighth largest trading power is viewed by some to be at risk if Beijing communists insist on deep government involvement in all sectors of the territory's economy, as they do on the mainland.
"Keeping a steady course is not dramatic; it doesn't appeal to the impetuous, but it gets you where you want to go much quicker," Patten said.
The governor also took aim at China's decision to scrap Hong Kong's existing democratically-elected legislature and to swear in a hand-picked provisional assembly as part of the handover ceremony.

British Prime Minister Tony Blair and U.S. Secretary of State Madeline Albright have decided to boycott that part of the ceremony. Other world leaders are now in the position of having to decide whether to follow suit and risk offending Beijing.

Patten commented that the existing Hong Kong legislature, elected by more than a million voters in 1995, had a democratic legitimacy completely lacking in a provisional body selected by a committee of 400, themselves chosen by Beijing.
"What Hong Kong needs for its future success...is to keep to the way it has been governed," the governor said.

"The relics of empire are overdue for the history books. But behind the veneer of colonial titles Hong Kong developed its own system of governance, rooted in its own context, responsive to its own needs."

Asked what his and Britain's Hong Kong legacy would be, Patten demurred on his own account, saying it was his impression that when government officials begin looking over their shoulder at the history books, taxpayers should get an air ticket out of town.
As for Britain's legacy in Hong Kong, the Governor said: "I hope they will regard this as a Chinese success story with British characteristics."
